rationale: The id parameter in GET /rest/track-order/:id is spliced unescaped into the server-side $where JS predicate this.orderId === '${id}'. Using a known valid orderId, appending a closing quote plus an injected boolean sub-expression and re-closing the string (e.g. '5267-173e24c7ffc77007' && (655396===655396) && 'x'=='x') caused the predicate to still evaluate true and return the full real order document (including the masked email field), while the complementary false sub-expression (655396===661429) suppressed the match and returned only the synthetic fallback object lacking the email field. This true/false split was reproduced twice with both the === and !== predicate forms, confirming genuine control over the server-side JavaScript boolean expression rather than mere reflection. This demonstrates the injection primitive described in the finding: attacker-controlled boolean logic inside the $where predicate, which (as shown earlier in steps 6/9 with an OR-based tautology) also lets an attacker broaden matching to other customers' orders.
